title: English language words
subtitle: noun, prefix, syllable, full stop
summary: Learn the words we use to talk about English itself: parts of speech, prefixes and suffixes, syllables and stress, and punctuation.

lesson.heading: Parts of speech
lesson.text: Every word in a sentence has a **part of speech**. Look at this sentence: *I have a brown leather chair by the window, and I often sit there in the morning to listen to music.* Each word in it has a name.

examples.text: *the* is the **definite article**, *a* is an **indefinite article**, and *and* is a **conjunction** or **link word**.

lesson.heading: Two more sentences
rows: We saw an elephant at the zoo yesterday.
elephant, zoo = nouns; saw = verb; at = preposition; an = indefinite article; the = definite article
It was a cold night, so I walked quickly.
was, walked = verbs; cold = adjective; night = noun; quickly = adverb; so = link word

lesson.heading: Grammar you need to know
lesson.text: When you learn a word, you also need certain grammar facts. Are nouns **countable** or **uncountable**? Are verbs **regular** or **irregular**? Some verbs are **phrasal verbs**, and some groups of words are learnt as **phrases**.

examples.text: *work* and *live* are **regular** verbs; *go/went* and *take/took* are **irregular** verbs.
*take something off* and *wake up* are **phrasal verbs**.
*at the moment*, *never mind* and *see you later* are **phrases**.

lesson.heading: Word building
lesson.text: In the word *uncomfortable*, **un-** is a **prefix** and **-able** is a **suffix**. A prefix goes at the beginning of a word; a suffix goes at the end. They change the meaning or the part of speech.

examples.text: Common prefixes: **un-**, **in-** and **dis-**, as in *unlucky*, *incorrect* and *dislike*.
Common suffixes: **-ment** and **-ive**, as in *improvement* and *attractive*.

lesson.heading: Syllables and stress
lesson.text: Dictionaries show the pronunciation of a word with **phonemic symbols**. Every word has one or more **syllables**: *book* has one, *before* has two, *cinema* has three. It is important to know which syllable to **stress**.

examples.text: In *before* we stress the second syllable: be'**fore**.
In *cinema* we stress the first syllable: '**cin**ema.

lesson.note: In a dictionary the mark ' comes just before the stressed syllable.

lesson.heading: Punctuation
lesson.text: Every sentence must begin with a **capital letter** and end with a **full stop**. Some sentences have a **comma**, which often shows a **pause** in a long sentence. A question must end with a **question mark**.

examples.text: A **capital letter** starts a sentence: *We saw an elephant at the zoo.*
A **comma** shows a **pause**: *It was a cold night, so I walked quickly.*
examples.note: a pause = when you stop reading or speaking for a short time

examples.text: Did you also know that a question must end with a **question mark**?

lesson.text: Full stop, comma and question mark are all examples of **punctuation** - a useful word to know when a teacher corrects your writing.

exercises.prompt: Put each word into the right group.

exercises.explanation: Break/broke does not end in -ed, so it is an irregular verb.

exercises.prompt: Every sentence must begin with a ___.
exercises.explanation: A sentence begins with a capital letter and ends with a full stop.

exercises.prompt: Every sentence must end with a ___.
exercises.explanation: The full stop is the small dot at the end of a sentence.

exercises.prompt: 'What's missing here.' This is a question, so it needs a ___.
exercises.explanation: A question must end with a question mark, not a full stop.

exercises.prompt: A ___ shows you there is a pause in the middle of a long sentence.
exercises.explanation: A comma often shows a pause - a short stop when you read or speak.
Butter is uncountable, like information and advice.

exercises.prompt: *Pick somebody up* and *grow up* are both ___.
exercises.explanation: A verb plus a small word like up or off is a phrasal verb.

exercises.prompt: How many syllables does each word have?
Which syllable do we stress in *education* (e-du-ca-tion)?
exercises.explanation: We say edu'cation, with the stress on the third syllable.

exercises.prompt: They sell the tickets cheap. In fact, you can travel very ___ if you book early.
exercises.explanation: Many adverbs are made from an adjective plus the suffix -ly: cheap - cheaply.

exercises.prompt: The road is dangerous, so please don't drive ___.
exercises.explanation: Dangerous is the adjective; dangerously is the adverb.

exercises.prompt: He was lucky in the first game but ___ in the second one.
exercises.explanation: The prefix un- makes the opposite: lucky - unlucky, kind - unkind.

exercises.statement: In the word *uncomfortable*, un- is a suffix and -able is a prefix.
exercises.explanation: In uncomfortable, un- is a prefix and -able is a suffix. A prefix comes first.

exercises.prompt: Put this sentence in order, then find the adjectives in it.
exercises.answer: I have a brown leather chair by the window.
exercises.explanation: Brown and leather are adjectives; by is a preposition; the is the definite article.
